strengths: No false criminal ban; private-site and event rules are separated from ordinary streets.
Causation is labeled (“Interpretation, not law”; bins support the habit without fully causing it).
No fake survey numbers, dates, or ordinances.
Ekiben-on-Shinkansen versus messy food on a packed commuter car is a defensible manners distinction.
verified: Eating while walking is generally not a crime on ordinary Japanese streets.
tabearuki (食べ歩き) is the ordinary Japanese term for eating while walking.
tachi-gui (立ち食い) is standing-and-eating, distinct from walking-eating.
meiwaku (迷惑) is everyday language for imposing trouble on others.
Public street bins are often scarce relative to many Western downtowns (reinforcing, not sole cause).
Festival streets and many fair stalls are socially set up for handheld food.
questionable: “Younger people may care less” — plausible generational hedge, not evidenced.
School lunch and cleaning time as a direct training pipeline into sidewalk tabearuki manners — interpretive, not documented causation.
unsupported: Locals who eat a supermarket bento through a station wicket “usually look slightly annoyed at themselves, not proud of a cultural exception.”

issues.problem: Self-annoyance is written as an observed typical reaction, but it is invented psychology.
issues.suggestion: Delete the face/mood claim; keep the situational contrast (tickets, bodies, rice).

issues.location: ## What Visitors Are Actually Seeing — younger people
issues.problem: Generational slack is asserted without a survey; the “may” hedge is the only thing keeping it acceptable.
issues.suggestion: Keep the hedge; do not upgrade to “young people don’t care.”
